claims.text: The initial as-solidified Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, homogeneous, supersaturated solid solution.
Sub-eutectic thermal annealing triggers phase segregation in the alloy.
Thermal aging promotes diffusion-driven segregation of Mg.
Mg segregation causes the nucleation and growth of Mg-enriched intermetallic compounds.
The precipitated Mg-enriched intermetallic phases form localized galvanic couples with the surrounding alloy.
The resulting electrochemical heterogeneity accelerates localized corrosion.
Intermetallic precipitation modifies oxide-scale formation during high-temperature oxidation.
Relative to the as-solidified alloy, the thermally aged alloy will have a higher corrosion rate.
The higher corrosion rate will be indicated by more rapid current-density increases in electrochemical tests.
Relative to the as-solidified alloy, the thermally aged alloy will exhibit altered high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
The thermally aged alloy will form less protective oxide scales than the as-solidified alloy.
The as-solidified homogeneous baseline has lower corrosion and oxidation rates than the aged state.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys with density below 6 g/cm3.
Restricting annealing to sub-eutectic temperatures produces metastable-phase decomposition rather than complete equilibrium restructuring.
Corrosion and oxidation behavior can be compared after salt-spray exposure and oxidation in air at approximately 700°C.
The kinetics of Mg segregation are not fully established.
The identity of the intermetallic phases formed during aging is not fully established.
Failure to detect Mg-enriched intermetallic formation after annealing would falsify the proposed transformation pathway.
No significant difference in corrosion kinetics or oxide-scale formation between annealed and as-solidified samples would falsify the predicted property effects.
